newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia holds first post-war elections.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia holds first post-war elections.

text.p: Yugoslavia on Sunday held its first elections since the Dayton accords brought peace to Bosnia and political analysts forecast that Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's coalition would triumph over opposition parties.

The polling for a federal parliament and municipal authorities began at 7 a.m. (0600 GMT) and was ending at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT). The opposition coalition at one point threatened to boycott the elections but relented after the authorities appointed their representatives to electoral commissions.
Official results were not due before Thursday but unofficial returns early in the week were likely to indicate the outcome.

Milosevic, blamed by the West for plunging old Yugoslavia into conflict, now presents himself as a man of peace and his ruling alliance of the Socialist party and two other parties made no campaign mention of the wars in Bosnia and Croatia.
"I am certain the elections are of great significance for the stability of the whole region," he told reporters after voting in Belgrade.
"I believe people know this very well and they will turn out in large numbers for today's elections," he added.
Milosevic was accompanied by his wife, Mirjana Markovic, a Marxist who heads one of three parties backing the president.
Voters queuing at polling stations voiced only bitterness about an election which they believed would change nothing.

"We will live like this all our lives if these people remain in power," said Dragan, 40, an electrician with an unemployed wife and teenage daughter. "With these authorities, there can be no revival of the economy or progress."
A year of peace and the end of a U.N. trade embargo has failed to bring economic relief to a country which once enjoyed the highest standard of living in Eastern Europe.
Almost a third of the population now lives in poverty, according to a Red Cross survey.
The opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, which attracted large crowds at rallies across the country, tried to capitalise on widespread discontent over the troubled economy.
But the coalition was hampered because the state media ignored it and by divisions within its own ranks.
Destitute Serb refugees from Croatia and Bosnia who might have caused political problems for Milosevic have no legal status and cannot vote in the election.

Although Milosevic is not a candidate in the polls, an election victory for his parties should enable him to push through constitutional change enabling him to stay in power after his second and final term as president expires next year.
Diplomats say he will probably assume the post of federal president after the next federal parliament invests the ceremonial post with strong executive authority.

A team of election observers from the United States and several other states from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) were monitoring voting at some of the 10,000 polling stations in Serbia and Montenegro, the two remaining Yugoslav republics.
